intro: A Cedar of Lebanon in the Arantzadi market gardens, about 200 years old, escaped being sold for toothpicks; the planes at the Curtidores bridge were planted in the mid-nineteenth century because the washerwomen on the Arga asked for shade; the palace sequoia lost its crown to lightning in 1933 and grew two more. The Taconera, the Ciudadela and the riverside paths hold the rest of the city's trees. Further out, 13 to 25 km into the valleys, stand five oaks Navarra has declared Natural Monuments. Twenty-five trees in all.
meta_description: A cedar saved from the toothpick trade, the washerwomen's planes on the Arga, a lightning-split sequoia. 25 old trees in and around Pamplona.
question_answer: The oldest tree near Pamplona is most likely the Roble de Orkin, a pedunculate oak in the Ultzama valley that is called millenary for its size, though nobody publishes an age for it. In the city itself the oldest dated tree is the Cedar of Lebanon at Arantzadi, which Pamplona's own 2010 book of old and singular trees puts at about 200 years.
question_meta: The Roble de Orkin is probably the oldest tree near Pamplona; in town, the Arantzadi cedar is about 200 years old. 25 trees, with directions.
question_context: Two sources cover Pamplona's trees, and they answer the age question differently. Pamplona's own book, Árboles viejos y árboles singulares de Pamplona, published by the city in 2010 with the Asociación de Amigos de los Árboles Viejos, catalogues more than 100 singular trees and 37 groups across some 50 species, and it is frank about the city. Its trees are young on the whole, the book says, and the few old ones may be 150 to 200 years. Dutch elm disease killed more than 11,000 of Pamplona's elms in 1985, several hundred of them over a century old. The oldest tree the book dates is the Cedar of Lebanon in the Arantzadi market gardens, at about 200 years. Navarra's register of 47 Natural Monuments, approved in its present form at the end of 2009, records species, place, year of declaration and a coordinate, and no ages at all. The oak at Orkin in the Ultzama valley, about 20 km north, is widely called millenary on the strength of its size, which is a reputation and not a measurement.

faq.a: In the Taconera gardens, the Ciudadela, Arantzadi and along the Arga at the Curtidores and San Pedro bridges. Pamplona's 2010 book of old trees puts the Arantzadi cedar at about 200 years, the Curtidores planes were planted in the mid-nineteenth century, and the sequoia in the garden of the Palacio de Navarra has stood there since 1855.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Pamplona?
faq.a: Probably the Roble de Orkin in the Ultzama valley, which is often called millenary because of its size; Navarra publishes no ages for its declared trees, so that is a reputation rather than a figure. In the city, the oldest dated tree is the Arantzadi cedar, at about 200 years.

In town, yes. The fifteen city trees all lie within about two kilometres of one another, from the Ciudadela, the Taconera and the palace garden on the high ground down to the Arga at the Curtidores bridge, the Rochapea and Arantzadi. The valley oaks are separate trips, 13 to 25 km out; only the two at Jauntsarats, about 570 metres apart, can be walked between.

Yes. The city trees stand in public parks and on the riverside path; the Ciudadela park is gated and keeps opening hours. The palace sequoia is in an enclosed garden and the yew stands on a roundabout, so both are seen from the street. The valley oaks stand on village common land and woodland with tracks to them.

faq.q: What does Natural Monument mean in Navarra?
faq.a: An individual legal declaration. Navarra has named 47 of them, most trees, each protected in its own right; the catalogue as it stands was approved at the end of 2009, extending a first group declared in 1991.

faq.q: Why are the valley trees mostly oaks?
faq.a: Because the wet valleys north of Pamplona are Atlantic rather than Mediterranean country and grow oak, and because the villages pollarded them for centuries for firewood and charcoal, cutting the crown back repeatedly. That produces a short, hugely thick trunk under a wide crown, which is the shape that later gets declared a monument.

trees.name: The Sequoia of the Palacio de Navarra

location.address: Garden of the Palacio de Navarra, Avenida Carlos III, 31002 Pamplona

trees.story:
Lightning took the top off this sequoia in 1933, and the tree grew two new ones. Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees records that the strike destroyed the crown and that two side branches took over as leaders. In 2007 the main leader was fitted with a lightning rod, which is the sort of care a tree earns once it has been hit.

It has stood on this spot since 1855, when it was transplanted from a garden in Irurita, in the Baztan valley north of Pamplona, as a plant that had come from California. Giant sequoia seed first reached Europe in 1853, so this was an early arrival by any reckoning, and it has had more than 170 years in the city since.

Its garden is the walled one behind the Palacio de Navarra on Avenida Carlos III, the seat of the regional government, which declared it a Natural Monument in 1991, among the first trees to get that status. It is the only one of Navarra's 47 declared trees inside a city. The trunk is 6.94 metres round and the tree 35.7 metres tall, and the book calls it a spectacular giant in the very heart of Pamplona.

The garden is enclosed, so this is a tree you see over the wall from the avenue rather than stand under. At that height, split crown and all, the view from the pavement does the job.
trees.access: Free to see from the street; the garden of the Palacio de Navarra is enclosed and not normally open, so this is a view rather than a visit
trees.transport: On Avenida Carlos III in the middle of Pamplona, a few minutes on foot from the Plaza del Castillo
trees.notes: Declared a Natural Monument of Navarra in 1991. Single-sourced from the Gobierno de Navarra SITNA register, which publishes species, place, declaration year and coordinate and no measurements, no age and no vitality field. Published as a view-only tree because the palace garden is enclosed; if it is open on some days, we would like to know. Árboles viejos y árboles singulares de Pamplona (Ayuntamiento de Pamplona with the Asociación de Amigos de los Árboles Viejos, 2010), p. 49: transplanted to its present place in 1855 from a garden in Irurita (the plant came from California); lightning in 1933 destroyed the crown and two side branches took over as leaders; Natural Monument 1991; lightning rod on the main leader 2007. p. 9: 'gigante espectacular en el mismo corazón de Pamplona'.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 35.7 metres, enough to see over the garden wall from the avenue, and by a top divided between two leaders. It stands in the enclosed garden of the Palacio de Navarra.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Gobierno de Navarra), M.N. 25, no. MN 25

trees.name: The Oak of Orkin
trees.age_estimate: often called millenary on the strength of its size, with no published figure

location.address: Arraitz-Orkin, Ultzama valley, 31797 Navarra

trees.story: This is the tree people in Navarra mean when they say the big oak. It stands at Orkin, in the Ultzama valley north of Pamplona, and it is habitually described as millenary, which is a reputation built on its size rather than any measurement: Navarra's register gives it a species, a place, a declaration year and a coordinate and nothing else, so nobody has published a girth, a height or an age for it. What is described consistently is the shape. It has been pollarded, cut back repeatedly over generations in the way Basque and Navarrese villages managed their oaks for firewood and charcoal, and the result is a broad rounded crown on a trunk that flares at the base into a mass of roots big enough that animals den in the gaps under them. Ultzama is wet Atlantic country, beech and oak and pasture rather than anything Mediterranean, 20 kilometres and a different climate from Pamplona. Navarra declared it a Natural Monument in 2009. If anybody has put a tape round it, we would like the number.
trees.access: Free, on village common ground in the Ultzama valley
trees.transport: Arraitz-Orkin, about 19 km north of Pamplona, then a short walk
trees.notes: Declared a Natural Monument of Navarra in 2009. The register publishes no height, girth or age, and the millenary description comes from popular and local accounts rather than a measurement, which is why the band here is very wide and the story says so. The pollarding and root-buttress description is from those same local accounts.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad, rounded, pollarded crown and a base flaring into a mass of roots big enough for animals to den in. It stands at Orkin, in the Ultzama valley.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Gobierno de Navarra), M.N. 43, no. MN 43

trees.name: The Oak of Eltzaburu

location.address: Eltzaburu, Ultzama valley, 31797 Navarra

trees.story: Lightning took one of its main limbs and it is still standing. The oak at Eltzaburu is reported at over 26 metres tall with a base close to two metres across, and it carries the marks of two separate attempts on its life: it escaped being felled, at some point nobody has dated, and it lost a major branch to a strike years ago. Navarra declared it a Natural Monument in 1991, in the first group, and it is number 10 on the list. It is the most reachable of the oaks on this page, because there is a marked walking route to it from the beech wood at Sastrain, which means somebody has decided people should come and look, and has put up signs. The Ultzama valley is the wet green half of Navarra, where the Atlantic weather gets over the watershed and beech and oak grow the way they do in the Basque country rather than the way they do on the Ebro. No age is published for it, as none is published for any of Navarra's 47 declared trees.
trees.access: Free, reached by a marked walking route from the beech wood at Sastrain
trees.transport: Eltzaburu, about 23 km north of Pamplona in the Ultzama valley
trees.notes: Declared a Natural Monument of Navarra in 1991, listed as number 10. The register publishes species, place, declaration year and coordinate only. The over 26 metres, the near two metre base, the lightning strike and the escape from felling come from Navarrese walking and heritage accounts rather than from the register, so height is carried and girth is not. No age published anywhere.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the gap where lightning took one of its main limbs, over 26 metres tall. It stands at Eltzaburu, reached by a marked route from Sastrain.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Gobierno de Navarra), M.N. 10, no. MN 10

trees.name: The Oaks of Jauntsarats

location.address: Jauntsarats, Basaburua valley, 31866 Navarra

trees.story: Two of them, declared separately, about 570 metres apart in the same wood. Navarra listed the oaks of Jauntsarats as Roble de Jauntsarats I and Roble de Jauntsarats II in 1991, giving each its own Natural Monument declaration rather than treating them as a pair, which is how this register works: it protects individuals and it does not group. They stand in the Basaburua valley in the wet northern country, in woodland rather than in the open, which is unusual for a Navarrese monumental oak; most of the declared ones are in pasture or on village common ground where they were kept as isolated trees for shade and fodder. Two giants inside a beech and oak wood are a different experience, because you come on them rather than see them from a distance. Navarra publishes no measurement and no age for either. This entry covers the first of the two and the second is 570 metres south; both are on the same walk, which makes Jauntsarats the only place near Pamplona where two declared Natural Monument trees can be seen in one outing.
trees.access: Free, in woodland on village ground in the Basaburua valley
trees.transport: Jauntsarats, about 25 km north of Pamplona
trees.notes: Two separate Natural Monument declarations of 1991, Roble de Jauntsarats I and II, 585 m apart by the register's own coordinates; this entry is the first, and the story says the second stands nearby. No measurements, no age and no vitality field in the register.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as one of two separately declared oaks about 570 metres apart, come upon inside the wood rather than seen from a distance. It stands at Jauntsarats.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Gobierno de Navarra), M.N. 8 (Jauntsarats I), no. MN 8

trees.name: The Oak of Azanza

location.address: Azanza, Goni valley, 31839 Navarra

trees.story: This one is a different oak from the others, and the difference is the whole reason it is worth a separate stop. Quercus pubescens, the downy oak, is the dry-country oak of southern Europe: smaller leaves with felted undersides, tolerant of thin limestone soils and long summers, and it takes over from pedunculate oak as you come south and west out of the Atlantic valleys. Azanza sits in the Goni valley on that boundary, in the hills below the Sierra de Andia, and the change in the trees over 20 kilometres of road from Ultzama is the clearest lesson in Navarrese geography anybody could ask for. Navarra declared this tree a Natural Monument in 2009 and, as with all 47, published a species, a place, a year and a coordinate and no measurements at all. That is the honest state of it: an officially protected oak of a species the north of Navarra does not grow, standing where two climates meet, and nobody has said how big or how old it is. If you have measured it, tell us.
trees.access: Free, on village ground in the Goni valley
trees.transport: Azanza, about 16 km northwest of Pamplona
trees.notes: Declared a Natural Monument of Navarra in 2009. Single-sourced from the SITNA register, which gives the species as Quercus humilis Mill., a synonym of Quercus pubescens, and publishes no height, girth or age. The climate-boundary reading is general biogeography of the species, not a claim about this individual.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its smaller leaves with felted undersides, a dry-country oak distinct from the pedunculate oaks further north. It stands at Azanza, in the Goni valley.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Gobierno de Navarra), M.N. 15, no. MN 15

trees.name: The Quejigo of Garinoain

location.address: Garinoain, Valdorba, 31395 Navarra

trees.story: Go south from Pamplona instead of north and the oaks change again. The quejigo, Quercus faginea, is the Iberian oak of the middle ground between the wet north and the dry Ebro plain: it holds its dead leaves through winter and drops them only when the new ones push, so a quejigo in February is a brown tree in a bare landscape, which is how you find one. This is the declared Natural Monument of the Valdorba, a district of small villages and Romanesque churches in the hills south of Pamplona that almost nobody visits, and Navarra listed it in 2009. Like every tree on this page it comes with a species, a place, a year and a coordinate and no measurements whatsoever. The Valdorba is worth the drive on its own account, and going out to look at a protected oak is as good a reason as any to end up in it. If you know its girth, or anyone has dated it, tell us and we will put the number on this page.
trees.access: Free, in open country in the Valdorba
trees.transport: Garinoain, about 25 km south of Pamplona
trees.notes: Declared a Natural Monument of Navarra in 2009. Single-sourced from the SITNA register: species, place, year and coordinate only, no measurements, no age, no vitality field. The winter marcescence described is standard for the species.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in winter by its dead brown leaves still on the branches, dropping only when new growth pushes them off. It stands at Garinoain, in the Valdorba.

official_register.name: Catalogo de Monumentos Naturales de Navarra (Decreto Foral 87/2009), M.N. 41, no. MN 41

trees.name: The Pollarded Poplar of Rochapea

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Rochapea, 31071 Pamplona

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 816492962, highway=footway).
trees.transport: In Rochapea, Pamplona; reachable on foot from the city centre along the riverside path, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Rochapea, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
Somebody cut the top off this poplar, and it grew to 26 metres anyway. Navarra's river-park register lists it as a trasmocho, a pollard: a tree beheaded at height so the regrowth can be cut again and again for firewood, fence posts and fodder. That is farm work rather than landscaping, and it means this trunk was earning its keep long before the banks of the Arga became a park. The register puts the trunk at 150 centimetres across, which works out at roughly four and a half metres round, and the 2013 survey that recorded it measured the height at 26 metres. Pollards are usually squat things. This one is not.

It stands on the riverside walk through Rochapea, the low district by the water where Pamplona came down from its walls to do its washing while the old town kept to the ridge. The path is free and open at any hour.

Two things we cannot tell you. Only the Navarra register describes this tree, so there is no second account to check it against, and that survey is now over a decade old. And nobody has recorded an age. Cutting a tree's head off scrambles the usual way of reading how long a poplar has stood, so we are not going to guess at one. If you know more about this tree, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the pollarded head, cut back at height with the regrowth rising out of it, on a trunk around four and a half metres round. It stands on the riverside path through Rochapea, on the bank of the Arga.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 1

trees.name: The Poplar of Txantrea

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Magdalena, Txantrea, 31004 Pamplona

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Same public footway confirmed via OpenStreetMap (way 816826057, highway=footway) as the London plane on the same stretch, about 80 metres away.
trees.transport: In the Magdalena area of the Txantrea district, Pamplona; reachable on foot along the riverside path, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Txantrea/Rotxapea, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
Navarra's register describes this tree in eight words, and then uses the same eight words for a different poplar a kilometre and a half away in Villava: a poplar of large diameter, over a metre through, vigorous. That is the entire official record of it. No height, no age, no story, and nothing that would tell it apart from its neighbours if you were standing under it.

What the phrase does give you is a floor. Over a metre of diameter means more than three metres around the trunk, and because the register stopped at the greater-than sign rather than taking the measurement, the real figure is probably larger than that. It is a big riverside poplar on a river that grows them.

It stands on the Magdalena stretch of the Arga in Txantrea, on the riverside path that runs the length of the valley through Pamplona, free and open at all hours. The plane tree with the old electrical cable brackets on its trunk is about 90 metres along the same path.

Only the register describes this tree, and its survey dates from 2013. Nobody has recorded an age for it, and nobody has taped the trunk properly either. If you have walked out and looked at it, tell us what you found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it only by where it stands, because nothing in the record separates it from the other big poplars here: on the Magdalena river walk in Txantrea, about 90 metres from the plane with old cable brackets on its trunk.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 8

trees.name: The Plane of Txantrea

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Magdalena, Txantrea, 31004 Pamplona

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Same public footway confirmed via OpenStreetMap (way 816826057, highway=footway) as the black poplar on the same stretch, about 80 metres away.
trees.transport: In the Magdalena area of the Txantrea district, Pamplona; reachable on foot along the riverside path, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Txantrea/Rotxapea, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
This plane tree once did a second job as a utility pole. Navarra's register records it as a large plane carrying old supports for electrical cables, the brackets still fixed to the trunk long after whatever they held came down. It is the kind of detail a register almost never gives, and it makes this the one tree on this stretch of the Arga you can identify without a map.

The measurements are respectable on their own. The register puts the trunk between 120 and 130 centimetres across, so somewhere between roughly 3.8 and 4.1 metres round, which is a serious plane by any standard and an unusually big one to find standing on a riverbank rather than on a boulevard.

Pamplona's own survey of its old trees writes warmly about the planes of the Rochapea bridge, shade for the women who washed clothes in the Arga, and about stands of roughly century-old planes along these banks. It never names this tree, so treat that as the mood of the place rather than as evidence about this trunk.

And that is the honest gap: the register is the only source that describes this specific tree, its survey dates from 2013, and nobody has recorded an age. The cable brackets, at least, are something anyone standing there can check. If you know more, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old electrical cable brackets still fixed to the trunk, and by being a plane among poplars, with patchy flaking bark and broad leaves. It stands on the Magdalena river walk in Txantrea.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 3

trees.name: The Poplars of Erripagaña

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Erripagaña, Burlada / Burlata, 31600 Navarra

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 704534922, highway=footway).
trees.transport: In Erripagaña, Burlada, one of Pamplona's comarca towns along the Arga; reachable on foot along the riverside path from Pamplona, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Burlada, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
A Lombardy poplar is usually a narrow column, the exclamation mark of the roadside. One of these two is close to four metres round.

The register records a pair at this point on the river path at Erripagaña, both of them large and both vigorous, and it takes the trouble to measure them separately: 120 centimetres across for the bigger trunk, 90 for the smaller. Converted, that is roughly 3.8 metres around the first and about 2.8 around the second. Both figures come from diameters rather than a tape passed round the trunk, so read them as close rather than exact. They stand together, which is why they are one entry here rather than two: you walk to one place and both are in front of you, the thick one and the merely large one.

The setting is the Arga on its way through Burlada, on the continuous riverside walk that runs from Pamplona out through the comarca towns. Free, open, flat, and about as easy a tree visit as this site has.

What nobody has written down is how old either of them is, and the only description of them anywhere is the 2013 register survey. If you know this pair, or have measured them, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by being two poplars standing together, one noticeably thicker than the other, the bigger close to four metres round and the smaller nearer three. They stand on the river path at Erripagaña, in Burlada.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 4

trees.name: The Broken-Limbed Poplar of Villava

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Villava / Atarrabia, 31610 Navarra

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 42943052, highway=footway), the same path segment as the southernmost of the three (about 60m south) and the Lombardy poplar at the north end (about 180m north).
trees.transport: In Villava / Atarrabia, one of Pamplona's comarca towns along the Arga; reachable on foot along the riverside path from Pamplona, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Villava, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
One of this poplar's three main limbs is dead, and the bark has come away from parts of the trunk. Navarra's surveyors catalogued it as a singular tree anyway, and wrote the damage into the record rather than around it: a poplar of large diameter, three main branches, one of them dead, partially debarked.

That description is worth more than a tidier one would be. Of the three big poplars on this stretch of the Villava riverside it is the only one you can identify from the path without counting your steps, because the others are recorded as nothing more than large and vigorous. A three-limbed crown with one bare limb in it, and pale wood showing through where the bark has gone, is a silhouette rather than a category.

The register gives the trunk as over a metre across without finishing the measurement, which puts it over three metres round at the very least and probably a good deal more. It stands on the public path along the Arga through Villava, free and open, flat walking from Pamplona.

The survey behind all of this dates from 2013 and no other source describes the tree, so the dead limb and the bare patches are thirteen years old as facts. Nobody has recorded an age either. If you walk out and see how it is doing now, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its three main limbs, one of them dead and bare, and by the patches where the bark has come away from the trunk. It stands on the river walk in Villava, the middle of the three poplars on that stretch.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 6

trees.name: The Poplar of Villava (south)

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Villava / Atarrabia, 31610 Navarra

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 42943052, highway=footway), the same path segment as the broken-limbed poplar (about 60m north) and the Lombardy poplar at the north end (about 240m north).
trees.transport: In Villava / Atarrabia, one of Pamplona's comarca towns along the Arga; reachable on foot along the riverside path from Pamplona, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Villava, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
Three poplars big enough to be catalogued stand within 250 metres of each other on the Villava riverside, and this is the one the surveyors had nothing particular to say about. Its entry in Navarra's register reads: poplar of large diameter, over a metre, vigorous. The same sentence, word for word, describes another poplar a kilometre and a half away in Txantrea.

So take the sentence for what it is. Over a metre across means over three metres round the trunk, and since the register stopped at the greater-than sign rather than finishing the measurement, that number is a floor and not a figure. Vigorous is the surveyor's word for a tree in good health in 2013.

What carries it is the walk. Villava sits on the Arga upstream of Pamplona, on the valley road that pilgrims have come down for a thousand years, and the riverside path through it is flat, free and continuous, with the broken-limbed poplar 60 metres north and a third big one 240 metres beyond that.

Nobody has dated this tree, nobody has measured the trunk properly, and no source but the register describes it at all. If you can add anything to that, we would like to hear it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by position and little else, since the record says only that it is large and vigorous: it is the southernmost of the three big poplars on the Villava river walk, about 60 metres from the one with a dead limb.

official_register.name: Arboles Singulares del Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona (Gobierno de Navarra, SITNA), no. 35300014 tree 7

trees.name: The Poplar of Villava (north)

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Villava / Atarrabia, 31610 Navarra

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 42943052, highway=footway), the same path segment as the broken-limbed poplar (about 180m south) and the southernmost of the three (about 240m south).
trees.transport: In Villava / Atarrabia, one of Pamplona's comarca towns along the Arga; reachable on foot along the riverside path from Pamplona, or by Pamplona urban bus (TCC network) to Villava, then a short walk to the riverbank.
trees.story:
The register gives this tree four words and no numbers: a Lombardy poplar of large diameter. Every other tree catalogued along this river carries a measurement of some kind, a height, a diameter, at least a greater-than sign. This one carries none, so we are not going to put a figure on the trunk. Large is what the surveyor wrote and large is what you get.

The form is the useful part. A Lombardy poplar grows as a tall narrow column rather than a spreading crown, which is what makes rows of them visible across a valley from a long way off, and a thick one is a column that has been standing a while.

It stands at the northern end of the Villava riverside path, about 180 metres beyond the middle of the other two catalogued poplars on that stretch, on the flat free walk that runs along the Arga from Pamplona out through the comarca towns.

Nobody has recorded an age for it, nobody has recorded a girth, and no source other than the 2013 register survey describes it at all. This is the thinnest record of the eight trees on this river. Anything you can add, we will take.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shape, the tall narrow column of a Lombardy poplar rather than a spreading crown. It stands at the north end of the Villava river walk, about 180 metres beyond the middle of the other two poplars there.

trees.name: The Poplars of Zabaldika

location.address: Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua (river walk), Zabaldika, Olloki, Esteribar, 31620 Navarra
location.neighbourhood: Zabaldika, Esteribar (comarca de Pamplona, not Pamplona itself)

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside footpath (Iruñerriko ibai-pasealekua / Parque Fluvial de la Comarca de Pamplona), open at all times. Confirmed as a public footway via OpenStreetMap (way 163401794, highway=footway).
trees.transport: In Zabaldika (Olloki), Esteribar municipality, at the eastern end of the river-park corridor, well outside Pamplona's built-up area; reachable only on foot or by car/bike along the riverside path, roughly 5km from the western end of this cluster (the pollarded poplar at Rochapea) and about 1.4km beyond the three Villava poplars. No urban bus service confirmed reaching this point; treat as the far end of a long linear walk or a separate short visit, not as an easy add-on to the others.
trees.story:
Nobody wrote down how many trees are here. The register's entry reads chopos de gran tamaño, large poplars, plural, with no count and no measurement attached to it. Elsewhere on this river the same surveyors were precise enough to record two trunks at one point and give a diameter for each. Here they saw a group worth cataloguing and left it at that, so it may be two poplars, it may be three, it may be a small stand, and we are not going to pick a number to make the page tidier.

What is certain is where they are. This is the far eastern end of the river park, at Zabaldika in Esteribar, where the Arga comes down out of the hills and the path has long since left Pamplona's streets behind. It is the one tree entry on this river that is a walk rather than a stroll, and it should be treated as its own outing rather than tacked onto the others at the end of a long afternoon.

No age, no girth, no height, no count, and no source but a 2013 survey. If you make it out there, tell us what is standing and how many. On this one, almost anything you can tell us is more than we have.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a group of large poplars rather than a single trunk, though nobody has recorded how many. They stand at the far eastern end of the river path, at Zabaldika in Esteribar, well beyond the Villava trees.

trees.name: The Cedar of Arantzadi
trees.age_estimate: about 200 years, by the city's 2010 book

location.address: Finca de Gurbindo, Arantzadi, 31014 Pamplona

trees.story:
A timber company once wanted to buy this cedar and turn it into toothpicks. The tree is still here because the company went bankrupt first.

The story comes from Pamplona's own survey of its old and singular trees, published by the city in 2010, which counts this Cedar of Lebanon among the oldest and grandest trees in Pamplona and puts it at about 200 years. That is the top of the city's range. The same book found Pamplona's trees young on the whole, with the few old ones somewhere between 150 and 200.

It stands by the Gurbindo farm in Arantzadi, the loop of the Arga below the old town where the city grows its vegetables, in market gardens the book calls a thousand years old. The name itself is on record from 1291 and means a thicket of thorns. The cedar has kept the gardeners company for about two of those ten centuries.

The book measured it at 4.94 metres round at chest height and 27.5 metres tall, with a crown 28 metres across, heavily branched in the flat tiers that set a Cedar of Lebanon apart from its relatives. Another big cedar of the same species stands across from the Arantzadi swimming pools, and the book reckons neither has anything to envy in the declared Natural Monument cedar at the Señorío de Bertiz, north of the city.
trees.access: Free; Arantzadi is a public park in the river meander. The cedar stands by the Gurbindo farm at the edge of the market gardens, so keep to the park paths rather than the cultivated plots
trees.transport: About 1.3 km north of the Plaza del Castillo, roughly 20 minutes on foot: down from the old town to the Arga and across into the Arantzadi meander
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, 28 metres across and built in flat horizontal tiers, over a trunk almost five metres round. It stands by the Gurbindo farm, beside the Arantzadi market gardens.
trees.notes: Single source, an official municipal publication: Árboles viejos y árboles singulares de Pamplona (Ayuntamiento de Pamplona with the Asociación de Amigos de los Árboles Viejos, 2010), p. 40 (about 200 years, the toothpick episode, girth 4.94 m at 1.30 m, height 27.5 m, crown 28.1 m, form 'muy ramoso'), p. 9 (the millenary market gardens), p. 10 (old trees in Pamplona 150 to 200 years), p. 19 (Arantzadi recorded 1291, 'espinar'). Age range 190 to 230 widens the book's 'about 200' for the years since 2010. trees.name: The Washerwomen's Planes of the Curtidores Bridge
trees.age_estimate: planted in the mid-19th century, by the city's 2010 book

location.address: Paseo fluvial del Arga at the Puente de Curtidores, 31014 Pamplona

trees.story:
These trees exist because the washerwomen of Pamplona asked for them. In the middle of the nineteenth century the women who did the city's laundry on the bank of the Arga wanted shade while they worked, and the planes were planted at their request.

The washing has long gone from the river. The trees have not. Pamplona's own book of old and singular trees, published by the city in 2010, counts the group at the Curtidores bridge at somewhere between 25 and 100 planes, and gives a sample trunk at 2.52 metres round and 20 metres tall. Planted around the middle of that century, they are some 160 to 180 years old, which in a city the same book found to have mostly young trees puts them among the elders.

The bridge joins the Rochapea, the low district on the north bank, to the Casco Viejo on its ridge, and the book reckons hundreds of people cross it every day. What they see is the detail the book singles out. The branches lean out and down until they brush the water.

The river is also taking something back. Erosion has been stripping the soil from the roots, which stand more exposed every year, as they do under other groups of planes along the Arga. A tree planted for women washing at the water's edge is slowly being undercut by the same water.
trees.access: Free, on the public riverside path along the Arga, open at all times
trees.transport: About 800 metres on foot from the Plaza del Castillo, roughly 12 minutes, down from the old town to the river at the Curtidores bridge
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the line of planes leaning out over the Arga, branches dipping to the water and roots bared by the current. They stand on the riverbank at the Curtidores bridge.
trees.notes: Group of trees (the book: 25 to 100 trunks), one place to stand at the bridge. trees.name: The Pollarded Planes of the Corralillos del Gas

location.address: Near the roundabout facing the Puente de Curtidores, Corralillos del Gas, Rochapea, 31014 Pamplona

trees.story:
These two planes outlasted the farmland they were cut for. They stand inside a stone enclosure near the roundabout that faces the Curtidores bridge, a pair of pollards that Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees calls born survivors of the recent urbanisation of the Rochapea.

The Rochapea, on the flat north bank of the Arga, was a farming district until not long ago. Pollarding belongs to that world. A tree is cut back well above the ground and the regrowth is harvested again and again, for firewood, poles or leaves for the animals, and over the years the trunk thickens beneath a crown of younger branches.

The book measured these at 7.1 metres round at chest height, 15 metres tall and 20 metres across the crown. It also records that the trunk forks from the base, so that girth may well take in more than one stem. Either way, size is half of why they are in the book. The other half is that nothing else like them stands anywhere around.

They are not quite alone in remembering the fields. About 80 metres away, a walnut in what is now a car park at the same spot, the Corralillos del gas, is in the book as one of the last witnesses of the market gardens. Nobody has dated the planes. If you know when they were first cut, tell us.
trees.access: Free, seen from the street and pavement; the two trees stand inside a stone enclosure
trees.transport: On the Rochapea side of the Curtidores bridge, about 15 minutes on foot from the Plaza del Castillo, down through the old town and over the Arga
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the stone enclosure around them, two pollarded planes, the measured trunk 7.1 metres round and forked from the base. They stand near the roundabout facing the Curtidores bridge.
trees.notes: Two trees in one enclosure, one place to stand. trees.name: The Tall Plane of the Isla de Arantzadi

location.address: Isla de Arantzadi, by the Puente de San Pedro, 31014 Pamplona

trees.story:
A plane tree more than 40 metres high stands on a scrap of island in the Arga, and the black poplar beside it, at 37 metres, is the shorter of the two.

The place is the isla de Arantzadi, by the San Pedro bridge, a patch of riverbank woodland where Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees finds ashes, willows, poplars, chestnuts, oaks and maples growing together. Two of them made the book. The plane, magnificent in its words, measured 3.5 metres round at chest height, which is not much waist for that much height. The poplar is the stouter tree, 5 metres round.

This ground was once an elm grove, and a few loose elms still stand among the rest. The book does not say what became of the others. It does record what happened to elms across the city. Dutch elm disease killed more than 11,000 of them in Pamplona in 1985 and left the city, in the book's word, half-naked. Several hundred of the elms lost in that decade were over a century old.

From the island the book points out the silhouettes of the giant sequoias, the Spanish fir and the holm oak at the Arantzadi swimming pools. Nobody has put an age on the plane. If you know it, tell us.
trees.access: Free, in the riverside green space by the San Pedro bridge, open at all times
trees.transport: About 15 minutes on foot north from the Plaza del Castillo, down from the old town to the Arga at the San Pedro bridge
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, over 40 metres, with the island's 37-metre black poplar beside it. It stands on the isla de Arantzadi by the San Pedro bridge.

trees.name: The Weeping Willow of the Ciudadela

location.address: Parque de la Ciudadela, Avenida del Ejército, 31002 Pamplona

trees.story:
Pamplona's newly-weds pick this tree for their wedding photographs, and it is a weeping willow, a species long held to stand for bitterness and unhappy love. Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees reports the first fact, and its own notes on the species supply the second, without remarking on the clash.

The willow grows inside the Ciudadela, the fortress the city built between 1571 and 1645, a fully walled pentagon that is now 28,000 square metres of park in the middle of Pamplona. Walls built to keep armies out now frame a backdrop for brides.

It is in the book for its form and spread rather than its height. The tree is 11 metres tall with a crown 17.4 metres across, far wider than it is high, and its long thin branches, which the book notes cannot carry their own weight, hang almost to the ground. The trunk is 2.3 metres round at chest height. The species has been cultivated for so long that its origin is hard to pin down, probably China, and it puts out yellow catkins between March and May, soon after the leaves.

Folklore had one more claim for it. Shelter under a weeping willow in a thunderstorm, the old belief went, and the lightning would pass you by. The book records that too.

Nobody has dated this willow. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.access: Free, in the public Ciudadela park; the park is gated and keeps opening hours
trees.transport: In the Ciudadela park, about 15 minutes on foot south-west of the Plaza del Castillo
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the long branches hanging almost to the ground from a crown 17 metres wide on an 11-metre tree. It stands in the Ciudadela park, where couples have their wedding photographs taken.

trees.name: The False Acacia on the Ciudadela Wall

location.address: Parque de la Ciudadela, on a mound of the wall, 31002 Pamplona

trees.story:
A tree from the eastern United States holds the high ground in Pamplona's sixteenth-century citadel. This false acacia, as the Spanish call the black locust, grows on top of a mound of the Ciudadela's walls, in the five-sided fortress the city built between 1571 and 1645, and Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees picks it out for two things, its size and its flowers in spring.

The size is 3.15 metres round at chest height and 19 metres tall on a single straight leader, with a crown 15.5 metres across. That makes it the larger of the book's only two entries for its species. The authors say so plainly. The tree is planted everywhere in gardens, yet apart from this one, a twisted group at the Caballo Blanco and some worth a mention under the walls on the Ronda Obispo Barbazán, they found no others in Pamplona worth the word singular.

The flowers come in hanging clusters, white and scented, and are popularly called pan y quesillo, bread and cheese, for their pleasant smell and taste. The book adds that the tree is generally toxic, so the nickname is as far as it should go. Its hard yellowish wood stands up to the weather well enough to be used for posts in farm fences.

On the same mound the book points out a group of pines and white poplars it also rates as spectacular. Nobody has given this tree an age. If you know it, tell us.

trees.name: The False Acacias of the Caballo Blanco

location.address: Caballo Blanco, Baluarte del Redín, Casco Viejo, 31001 Pamplona

trees.story:
The medieval building beside these trees went up in the 1960s, put together from the remains of an old palace on the calle Nueva. The trees around it are the genuinely old part of the scene.

This is the Caballo Blanco, at the Redín corner of the city walls, which Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees calls one of the most beautiful and unusual places in the city. A group of false acacias grows here, somewhere between four and ten of them, and the book chose them for one quality, the beauty of their twisted form in a singular setting. Old, contorted trunks, it says, that bring beauty and colour to the place. The trunk it measured is 2.98 metres round at chest height and 17 metres tall. The species grows strong, tortuous branches by habit, and these have had the time to make the most of it.

The authors admit that the best thing here is not the trees but the view. The sixteenth-century Redín bastion makes a lookout over Monte Ezkaba, Arantzadi and the districts of the Rochapea and the Chantrea, the river country below the walls where several other trees on this page stand. Close by, in the inner courtyard of the old teacher training college, the book notes a big sequoia as well.

Nobody has put an age on the acacias. If you know it, tell us.

trees.name: The Weeping Pagoda Tree of the Café Vienés

location.address: Parque de la Taconera, beside the Café Vienés, 31001 Pamplona

trees.story:
Pamplona's own book of old trees suggests looking at this one over a coffee. It stands beside the Café Vienés in the Taconera, and the city's 2010 survey of old and singular trees calls it worth admiring while you drink one.

It is a weeping, twisted form of the Japanese pagoda tree, and the book counts it among the most beautiful and spectacular in Pamplona. Nothing about it is big. The trunk is 1.5 metres round at chest height and splits three ways, and the tree stands 9.5 metres tall under a crown 10 metres across. What earns the entry is the shape, the branches bending and hanging rather than reaching.

In China and Japan the species is planted beside temples and tombs. Here it gets a café terrace, in a park whose name is older than any tree in it. The Taconera is on record from 1276, and linguists read the word as a place of stumps, tocones, left by trees cut down long before. For centuries after that the ground held vineyards and cereal. Only when the city's walls were extended to take it in did trees return, and by 1558 the council had appointed a guard for the young ones planted here.

Several more weeping pagoda trees grow around the Taconera, but this is the one the book chose. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Taconera

location.address: Parque de la Taconera, right of the main entrance, 31001 Pamplona

trees.story:
Both of California's great redwoods grow within a few steps of each other just inside the Taconera, and Pamplona's 2010 book of old and singular trees sends you there to compare them. On the right of the main entrance stands the giant sequoia the book measured. Close by are two more giant sequoias and a coast redwood.

The difference is easy to see once you know where to look. A giant sequoia carries short, scale-like needles pressed along the shoot. A coast redwood has flat needles set in two rows, more like a yew. The giant sequoia is the bulkier species. The coast redwood is the taller.

This one is 4.26 metres round at chest height and 26 metres tall, on a single straight leader, with a crown 12.9 metres across. That is respectable rather than enormous. Pamplona's best-known sequoia stands about 600 metres east in the garden of the Palacio de Navarra, almost seven metres round, and that one has been in the city since 1855.

The Taconera has been looking after trees for a long time. The council appointed a guard for its newly planted trees in 1558, and by 1564 it was paying a caretaker 20 pounds a year to look after them. In December the book records flocks of starlings from northern Europe coming in at dawn and dusk to roost in the park.

Nobody has dated this sequoia. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

trees.transport: In the Taconera gardens on the western edge of the old town, about 10 minutes on foot west of the Plaza del Castillo; the tree is on the right as you come in by the main entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the short, scale-like needles and the single straight trunk, 4.26 metres round. It stands on the right of the Taconera's main entrance, near two more giant sequoias and a coast redwood.

trees.name: The Ash of the Parque del Runa

location.address: Parque del Runa, Rochapea, 31014 Pamplona

trees.story:
This ash is 5.25 metres round at chest height, and that is not even why it is in the book. Pamplona's 2010 survey of old and singular trees chose it for its form of growth, which it records in one word, recepado. That is a tree cut back low on the trunk so that it sprouts again, a treatment ash takes better than most. What came back is 19 metres tall with a crown 18.4 metres across, nearly as wide as it is high. A trunk regrown from a cut can carry several stems, so the girth may well take in more than one.

Ash was a working tree. The book notes that its wood is flexible and tough, which made it the wood for tool handles, and that its leaves fed livestock, the branches cut at height in the way called trasmoche. Old ashes, it adds, often turn up beside shepherds' huts. Whether this one was cut for wood or for fodder, the book does not say.

The ground suits the story. The Parque del Runa lies in the Rochapea, on the flat north bank of the Arga, a district the same book describes as farming country until its recent urbanisation. In Navarra the common ash belongs to the wetter Atlantic north, along rivers such as the Bidasoa, and it likes fresh, deep soil.

Nobody has put an age on it. If you know this tree's history, tell us.
trees.access: Free, in a public park in the Rochapea, open at all times
trees.transport: In the Rochapea, a short walk from the Curtidores bridge, about 15 minutes on foot from the Plaza del Castillo
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, 18 metres across on a 19-metre tree, over a trunk cut back low and regrown, 5.25 metres round. It stands in the Parque del Runa in the Rochapea.

'Recepado' read with the RAE sense of 'recepar' (cut low on the trunk so it resprouts). trees.name: The Yew of the Tres Reyes Roundabout

location.address: Roundabout in front of the Hotel Tres Reyes, Jardines de la Taconera, 31001 Pamplona

trees.story:
This yew lives on a traffic roundabout, and Pamplona's town plan protects it as a listed element at grade 2. The city's 2010 book of old and singular trees calls it an elegant landmark in the middle of town and, in its introduction, a born survivor against the advance of asphalt.

That is a fair description of a tree whose neighbours are lanes of cars. It stands in front of the Hotel Tres Reyes, which went up in 1962 on part of the Bosquecillo, a wooded triangle of the Taconera gardens where, the book records, there had been a dovecote and a pond with ducks and sometimes swans.

The trunk is modest, 1.83 metres round at chest height on a single leader, with a crown 13.5 metres across. The height is another matter. At 16.5 metres it is taller than the 10 to 15 metres the book gives as what a yew usually reaches, often as little more than a shrub.

Yews are among the longest-lived trees in Europe, and the book is candid that the mountains of Navarra hold far bigger and older ones than anything in the city. Every part of the tree is poisonous except the red flesh around the seed, and its tough, springy wood once made bows.

The same roundabout holds hackberries that the book also lists as singular. Nobody has dated the yew. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.access: Free to see from the pavement; it stands on a traffic roundabout, so it is a view rather than a visit
trees.transport: At the Hotel Tres Reyes on the edge of the old town, about 7 minutes on foot west of the Plaza del Castillo, next to the Taconera gardens
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the dark evergreen conifer on the roundabout, 16.5 metres tall on a single trunk, among the hackberries. It stands in front of the Hotel Tres Reyes.
